Bite 01
The Need for Systematic Study of God’s Word
  I.Introduction


 II.Two Basic Questions You Must Answer 
A.Why is it that people do not study the Bible?
1.They do not place it on their priority list.
2.They believe it is not relevant for today.
3.They do not know how to begin to study it.
4.They do not think they can understand it on their own.

B.Why do we need to study the Bible?
1.1 Peter 2:2

The Bible was not written to satisfy your curiosity, but to make you conform to Christ’s image. Not to make you a smarter sinner, but to make you like the Savior. Not to fill you head with a collection of biblical facts, but to transform your life.1 Therefore, putting aside all malice and all guile and hypocrisy and envy and all slander, 2 like newborn babes, long for the pure milk of the word, that by it you may grow in respect to salvation. . . .
a.Attitude
b.Appetite
c.Aim
We are to grab for the Word as a baby grabs for a bottle (attitude). We must crave the Word (appetite). We must focus on growing, not just knowing (aim).

Answer #1It is the only means for spiritual growth!

2.Hebrews 5:11-14
Concerning him we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing. For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you have need again for someone to teach you the elementary principles of the oracles of God, and you have come to need milk and not solid food. For everyone who partakes only of milk is not accustomed to the word of righteousness, for he is a babe. But solid food is for the mature, who because of practice have their senses trained to discern good and evil. 
a.The problem with the audience here is not the difficulty of the revelation, but the density of the reception. There is a learning disability.
b.Those mature in Christ are those who by constant use have trained themselves to take the Word and use it in their lives to distinguish good and evil.
c.The best standard for spiritual maturity is not how much you know and understand; it is how much you use what you know and understand.
d.The opposite of ignorance in the spiritual realm is not knowledge; it is application.
Answer #2It is the divine means to develop spirituality!
3.2 Timothy 3:16-17
All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness; that the man of God may be adequate, equipped for every good work. 
It is profitable for teaching/doctrine.
It will structure your thinking, because what we believe determines how we live.
b.It is profitable for reproof/rebuke.
It will tell us when we are out of bounds.
c.It is profitable for correction.
It will not only reveal our problems, it will also solve them.
d.It is profitable for training in righteous living.
The end result of the effects of God’s Word is that we will be equipped/prepared for every good work.

Answer #3It is the only means for preparation for ministry and life!

Would you let a surgeon operate on you if he knew just as much about medicine as you know of God’s Word?




III.Summary
Why do we need to study the Scriptures? There are three basic reasons.
A.It is essential to GROW us.


B.It is essential to MATURE us.


C.It is essential to PREPARE us.


The Bible is not for your INFORMATION,
It is for your TRANSFORMATION!

(The Definition)
Introduction

  I.The Definition of the Process
A.Bible study is methodicalness.
[Certain steps in a certain order to guarantee a certain result.]

a.Personal study of the Scriptures
b.Study that produces life change

What? What do I see?
b.Step TWO: Interpretation
What does it mean?
c.Step THREE: Application
What does it mean to me? How does it work?

B.Bible study is methodicalness with a view to becoming receptive and reproductive.
[Before we can make an impact on our culture, the Scripture must make an impact on our lives.]
Involvement in the world.

2.Isolation from the world.

Four reasons why firsthand discovery of the Scriptures is essential:
1.It will enable you to think for yourself.
[The Bible was not given as a riddle, but as a Revelation.]
2.It will prepare you to evaluate the thoughts of others.

3.It will give you the joy of personal discovery.

4.It will enable you to fall in love with the Author.

Bite 03
The Process of Systematic Study of God’s Word
(The Details)
  II.The Process of Bible Study
A.Step one: Observation ― “What do I see?”
There are four basic things to notice:
1.Terms
Terms – Terms are more that just words. Terms have specific meaning based on their context. 
2.Structure
a. Grammatical structure tells us important information like subject, verb, etc.

b.Literary structure reveals clues through recognition of things like questions and answers; cause and effect; etc.

3.Literary form (genre)
Are we looking at poetry, prophecy, history, narrative, etc.?

4.Atmosphere
Tells us the feelings, mood, tone, environment, etc. What was it like to be in the author’s shoes?
B.Step two: Interpretation ― “What does it mean?”
There are three things that will aid us in the discovery of the meaning of a passage.
1.Bombard the text with questions. The Bible is never embarrassed to be asked questions.

2.Look for the answers. These most often will come out of our observation process.

3.Integrate the parts and put them together. Put all the details together into a meaningful whole.
The more time you spend in observation, the less time you will spend in interpretation, and the more accurate will be your results.


Step three: Application ― “How does it work?”
1.How does it work for me?

2.How does it work for others?

Bite 05
The Specifics of Reading
(First Five Rules for Reading)
Introduction

  I.Read the Bible thoughtfully.
The Bible does not yield its fruits to the lazy. We must program our minds with the Word.
If you seek her as silver, 
And search for her as for hidden treasures; 
Then you will discern the fear of the Lord, 
And discover the knowledge of God. (Proverbs 2:4-5; cf. Job 28)

 II.Read the Bible repeatedly.
A.Read all of one book in one setting.
B.Read each book from the beginning.


III.Read the Bible patiently.
Most people quit too soon before they find gold.


 IV.Read the Bible selectively.
Six questions will help you if you ask them.
A.#1:Who?
What is said about them?
What do they say?

B.#2:What?
What is happening here? What is the argument? What is the author trying to say?

C.#3:Where?
Where is my atlas?
D.#4:When?
Always determine what time it is. When did it happen? What happened before and after? When will these things take place?

E.#5:Why?
Why is this included? Why did it happen? Why did God allow it to happen?

F.#6:Wherefore? (So what?)
What difference does it make? Since it was written to change our lives, what difference will it make?

  V.Read the Bible prayerfully.
Learn to pray
Listen to new converts, children
Turn Scripture into prayer

Bite 08
The Cruciality of Structure

Introduction
Observation involves two propositions:
1.  Learn to read.
2.  Learn to detect structure.

  I.The Definition of Structure
Structure involves the relation and interrelation of component parts
Whenever you have two of anything (terms, phrases, clauses, prepositions, connectives, sentences, paragraphs, chapters, etc.) you have structure.
A.What God has said (= content)
B.How God has said it (= form)
1.Relationships
2.Arrangement

 II.The Kinds of Structure
A.Grammatical
One communicates his mind through his grammar
1.Verbs
2.Subject/object
3.Modifiers
4.Dependent and independent clauses
5.Phrases, especially prepositional phrases
6.Connectives / “signposts”
B.Literary (Genre)
A book presupposes unity.
III.The Spheres of Structure
A.Within a paragraph, primarily grammatical
(Worm’s Eye View)

B.Between paragraphs, primarily literary
(Bird’s Eye View)


IV.The Principles of Structure
A.The paragraph is the basic unit of study and thought
Not the verse or chapter
Not inspired, thus evaluate and change if warranted
A paragraph is a group of related sentences/ideas dealing with one leading topic or idea. It may have sub-thoughts, but they are always units. 

B.Devise a title for each paragraph
Value = a handle, means of review and recapitulation
Characteristics 
Brief
Personal
Memorable
Unique to that paragraph
Goal = develop “at homeness” in the book

C.The thought patterns are carried forward by five primary factors
1.Key persons ─ biographical structure
2.Key places ─ geographical structure
3.Key events ─ historical structure
4.Key ideas ─ ideological structure
5.Key times ─ chronological structure

D.Always look for elements of commonality that integrate a passage
(paragraph, segment, section, book, etc.)

V.The Laws of Structure
A.Law of Comparison = “the association of like things”
Note: Hebrews 5:10; cf. 5:5 “so also”

B.Law of Contrast = “the association of opposites”
Note: Romans 5:12-21
     12 Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, because all sinned— 13 for until the Law sin was in the world, but sin is not imputed when there is no law. 14 Nevertheless death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the offense of Adam, who is a type of Him who was to come.
     15 But the free gift is not like the transgression. For if by the transgression of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one Man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many. 16 The gift is not like that which came through the one who sinned; for on the one hand the judgment arose from one transgression resulting in condemnation, but on the other hand the free gift arose from many transgressions resulting in justification. 17 For if by the transgression of the one, death reigned through the one, much more those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the One, Jesus Christ.
     18 So then as through one transgression there resulted condemnation to all men, even so through one act of righteousness there resulted justification of life to all men. 19 For as through the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the One the many will be made righteous. 20 The Law came in so that the transgression would increase; but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, 21 so that, as sin reigned in death, even so grace would reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

C.Law of Repetition = “the reiteration of the same terms, phrases, clauses, etc.”
Note: Leviticus where “holy” is mentioned numerous times
Note: Hebrews 11  “faith”

D.Law of Continuity = “the repeated use of similar terms, phrases, clauses, etc.
Note: Luke 15 and the three “lost” parables.

E.    Law of Continuation = “the extended treatment of a particular aspect; the carrying through to its completion of an idea or series of events”
Note: This law is sometimes related to that of continuity, but it involves extension rather than recurrence. Cf. Genesis 13-14 and Genesis 18-19.

F.    Law of Climax = “the arrangement of material in such a way as to progress from the lesser to the greater and ultimately to the greatest”
Note: Exodus (especially 40:34-35)

G.Law of Cruciality = “the utilization of the principle of the pivot”
Note: The subject matter is arranged so that it turns around or upon some one factor. Cf. 2 Samuel (pivot is 11-12)

H.Law of Interchange = “the exchanging or alteration of certain elements”
  Note: Interchange is often utilized to strengthen contrasts or comparisons. Cf. 1 Samuel 1-2; Luke 1-2

I.   Laws of Particularization and Generalization = “the movement from the general to the particular, and from the particular to the general”
Note: Matthew 6:1-18 (particularization) and James 2 (generalization)

J.   Laws of Causation and Substantiation = “the progress from cause to effect, and from effect to cause”
Note: Romans 1:18-32 (causation) and Romans 8:18-30 (substantiation)
     18 For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth in unrighteousness, 19 because that which is known about God is evident within them; for God made it evident to them. 20 For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood through what has been made, so that they are without excuse. 21 For even though they knew God, they did not honor Him as God or give thanks, but they became futile in their speculations, and their foolish heart was darkened. 22 Professing to be wise, they became fools, 23 and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for an image in the form of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed animals and crawling creatures.
     Therefore God gave them over in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, so that their bodies would be dishonored among them. 25 For they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.
     26 For this reason God gave them over to degrading passions; for their women exchanged the natural function for that which is unnatural, 27 and in the same way also the men abandoned the natural function of the woman and burned in their desire toward one another, men with men committing indecent acts and receiving in their own persons the due penalty of their error.
     28 And just as they did not see fit to acknowledge God any longer, God gave them over to a depraved mind, to do those things which are not proper, 29 being filled with all unrighteousness, wickedness, greed, evil; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malice; they are gossips, 30 slanderers, [v]haters of God, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, 31 without understanding, untrustworthy, unloving, unmerciful; 32 and although they know the ordinance of God, that those who practice such things are worthy of death, they not only do the same, but also give hearty approval to those who practice them. (Romans 1:18-32)

K.    Law of Instrumentation = “the setting forth of the means to an end as well as the end itself”
Note: Involves the factor of purpose. Cf. John 20:30-31

L.    Law of Explanation or Analysis = “The presentation of an idea or event followed by its interpretation”
Note: Mark 4 (also, closely related to Law of Particularization)

M.   Law of Preparation or Introduction = “the inclusion of the background or setting for events or ideas”
Note: Prepares reader to understand that material that follows by that which precedes. Cf. Genesis 2:4-25 with Genesis 3

N.    Law of Summarization = “the employment of an abridgement of compendium either preceding or following a unit of material”
Note: Joshua 12

O.Law of Interrogation = “the use of a question or problem followed by its answer”
Note: Romans 6-7

P.Law of Harmony = “the effecting of unity by means of agreement”
Note: Assumes consistency. Cf. Romans 1:18-3:20 with 3:21 ff


Q.Law of Proportions = “the notion that emphasis is related to space given”
Note: Luke 9:51-19:27 (cf. Matthew with 2 chapters and Mark with 20 verses)

The Value and Method of Making Charts
Introduction


  I.The Place of the Chart in Relation to Other Methods
A.It is only one way of summarizing, recording, and preserving one’s findings and one’s thoughts.


B.It is not intended to eliminate but rather to supplement other methods such as the outline, enumerative summary, abstract, digest, essay, thesis, paraphrase, memorizing, examination, question, the underlined or annotated text, etc.


C.It is like a mariner’s map to aid in navigating the oceans of words, pages, books, ideas, men, events, etc.



 II.Some of the Advantages of the Chart
A.It appeals to the eye gate. Pictures are more readily remembered than words.
B.Its capacity to reveal the operation of or to apply the laws of composition and of the mind.
1.Perspective: seeing things as a whole; the sum of the parts
2.Principality: recognizing unity, centrality of feature, dominant purpose or idea; details subordinated into their larger patterns
3.Comparison: contact illuminates distinctive qualities and ideas
4.Repetition: often gives clue to organization and purpose
5.Proportion: what an author expands or what he abbreviates often reflects his aims.
6.Emphasis: he may emphasize by contrast, by proportion, by language, by repetition, by position, by atmosphere in attaining his aims.
7.Association: closely related to observation, prerequisite to understanding, indispensable to thinking, and an aid to memory

C.Its Economy and Value
1.For the viewer
ideas at a glance
strength of the impression
delivers from the quagmire of detail onto the highway of the dominant idea, the stepping stones to the significant, a guiding star to the overall plan
2.For the chart-maker
same as above, but more so
economy of mechanical process, provides a means of note-taking and recording of ideas with a minimum of writing
a minimum of interference with the apperceptive processes
3.For everyone
more portable
economy of memory, less forgetting because of emphasis on the visual, upon the above laws, and upon thinking (for the consumer, depreciator, and the dissipater of mental material)


III.The Nature of a Chart
A.In general, it should be simple, clear, graphic, intelligent, reveal the dominant aims and ideas. It should synthesis as well as analyze; generalize even more than particularize; characterize as well as itemize; describe as well as record.

B.In specific, it may show:
Main divisions of a book, a subject, a period of history.
Themes of organizing purpose; how the parts contribute to theme.
Pivotal events or key chapters, verses, phrases, and climax.
Who? ─ persons; What? ─ events; Where? ─geography; When? ─time element.
Literary features: stories poems, laws, descriptions, figures of speech, distinctive vocabulary, quotable passages, etc.
Comparison of the beginning and the end of a book.
Chapter titles, perhaps paragraph titles.
Relation to other books; relation to contemporary events, persons, etc.
Characteristics of sections and of book as a whole.
Topical studies: God, man, sin, holiness, law, sacrifice, suffering, justice, righteousness, prophets, priests, kings, the covenant, chosen people, etc.
List of summary observations (especially with topical studies where there is much detail: to answer, “what is the significance of this?”)
Choice quotations or descriptive phrases from secondary sources indicate sources; put your name and the date in upper, right corner.

IV.The Contents of a Chart
A.Take a sheet of paper (A4), not larger than two sheets
B.Draw a line the long way on the paper. This is your baseline
C.Read or scan material rapidly and mark on chart as you go main features, chapters, events. Note any turning points or divisions.
D.Read again to group related chapters. Fix more accurately divisions and sub-divisions. Note key expressions, phrases, characteristics in appropriate places. Seek to grasp the progressive steps in the attainment of the author’s purpose. Organize the whole around the climax of the book or topic or period.
E.Keep thinking backward and forward in the book. Connect related passages by arrows or in some way make them stand out together to the eye.
F.Keep note of special topics, and at the appropriate time work these out on your chart. If these involve considerable detail, use catchwords or phrases to bring to mind the detail and then draw up a short list of summary observations on the topic; findings and their significance.
G.Incorporate choice descriptive sentences from secondary or other sources.
H.Keep details subordinate. Ponder significance as wholes, units, and larger relationships. Be inductive. Seek to move from particular to general.
V.Some “Do’s” and “Don’ts’s” in Charting
A.    Don’t make it too large. Do keep it convenient to work on ─ seeable at a glance.
B.    Don’t make it too elaborate. It is better to make several, each featuring one or two ideas than to have it over-complicated to the loss of a chart’s advantage.
C.    Don’t let the mechanics of it usurp the ratiocinative! Observation and thought are requisite to valuable construction. Do keep it neat and orderly, but useful and practical.
D.    Don’t let your imagination get out of control, but do cultivate a disciplined imagination, an independent judgment, a fruitful creativity and originality.
E.    Don’t give way to designs that convey only the obvious and obscure the really significant. Do make it meaningful.
F.    Don’t get sidetracked by details, minor points, or controversial issues. Do keep on the main thoroughfares.
G.    Don’t be discouraged by your first attempts. Do try again. Remember that charts are valuable not only in studying but in teaching. Keep making charts. Study method continually. Do use other methods as well.
H.    Don’t forget to indicate sources. Do include source references and give quotations exactly in quotation marks with author, title, and page of book.
I.     Don’t forget to put your name and the date in upper, right-hand corner on front side. Do cultivate certain habits of orderly procedure.
Don’t roll. Do fold if too large.
K.    Don’t proceed chapter by chapter, but paragraph by paragraph. Do give each paragraph equal space.
L.Don’t be too wordy. Do make sure each paragraph title is a summary only.
M.Don’t make it bland. Use color, alliteration, pictures, etc. to communicate.

The Literary Background
(Genre = Narrative)

Introduction

  I.Suggestions for Biblical Narrative
A.Play close attention to the setting (especially details) of the narrative
1.The physical setting
2.The temporal setting
3.The cultural setting
B.Get to know the characters of the story as thoroughly as possible
1.The source of information
a.Direct descriptions
b.Responses of others to the character
c.Words and thoughts of the characters
d.Self-characterization
e.Actions of the character (subjective)
2.The subjects of the protagonist and the antagonist
a.Protagonist (hero of the story)

b.Antagonist (character or event)
(that which provides comparison/contrast against the protagonist)


C.Identify the nature of the plot development
(plot = arrangement of events)

III.Pondering the Parables
A.    The Definition: Parable = a figurative, fictional narrative which is true to life and designed for the historical and pedagogical purposes of conveying through analogy some specific spiritual truth, usually relative to the kingdom program of God.
B.The relevant Scripture:
10 And as soon as He was alone, His followers, along with the twelve, began asking Him about the parables. 11 And He was saying to them, “To you has been given the mystery of the kingdom of God; but those who are outside get everything in parables, 12 in order that while seeing, they may see and not perceive; and while hearing, they may hear and not understand lest they return and be forgiven.” 13 And He said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? And how will you understand all the parables?” (Mark 4:10-13a)
33 And with many such parables He was speaking the word to them as they were able to hear it; 34 and He did not speak to them without a parable; but He was explaining everything privately to His own disciples. (Mark 4:33-34)
9 And His disciples began questioning Him as to what this parable might be. 10 And He said, “To you it has been granted to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest it is in parables, in order that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.” (Luke 8:9-10)
10 And the disciples came and said to Him, “Why do You speak to them in parables?” 11 And He answered and said to them, “To you it has been granted to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been granted. 12 For whoever has, to him shall more be given, and he shall have an abundance; but whoever does not have, even what he has shall be taken away from him. 13 Therefore I speak to them in parables; because while seeing they do not see, and while hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. 14 And in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is being fulfilled, which says,
You will keep on hearing, but will not understand;
And you will keep on seeing, but will not perceive; (Matthew 13:10-14)
34 All these things Jesus spoke to the multitudes in parables, and He did not speak to them without a parable, 35 so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying, 
I will open My mouth in parables; 
I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world. (Matthew 13:33-35)
C.The purposes of a parable
1.Revelation: to reveal new truth to the responsive
2.Judgment:to conceal truth (of the kingdom) from the unresponsive
3.Persuade:to evoke decisions from the undecided
4.Perpetuate:to allow memory of the truth in a concrete form or story
D.The guidelines for interpreting parables
1.Recover the original setting of the parable
(historical and cultural contexts)
2.Discover the problem that is being answered
(relationship to the Kingdom)
3.Uncover the central truth of the parable
(major points(s) of comparison)
4.Relate the details to the central truth
(supporting scenery for the analogy)
5.State the intended appeal
(application in historical and contemporary setting)

B.Characteristics of visionary literature (Biblical apocalyptic)
1.   Structure: places a kaleidoscope structure of self-contained units
2.   Symbolism: communicates historical realities through ideological rather than literalistic symbols
3.   Supernatural:portrays a supernatural or transcendental world with divine, demonic, or angelic agencies
4.   Scope: transforms the known or present state of things into a situation that can only be imagined at the time of writing
5.   Subjects: includes the familiar in juxtaposition to the familiar of both people and places
6.   Scope: Scenic: reveals cosmic rather than a localized scene(s)
7.   Strangeness: characterizes pe0ple, settings, and events in extraordinary descriptions of reality



C.Principles for interpreting visionary literature
1.   Visionary material should be interpreted in relation to its own self-contained unit and then related to the larger context of the section or book in which it is found.
2.   Biblical symbols should be interpreted according to the “analogy of faith” (in comparison with other usages and symbols.
3.   Visionary literature anticipates the divine intervention of God for the salvation or judgment of men and nations.
4.   Visionary literature is primarily futuristic in its reference and uses present images to reveal the future unknowns, especially as they relate to the Day of the Lord.
5.   Familiarity with the whole of prophetic literature in the Bible protects from individual spiritualization and gives one the ability to distinguish near and far fulfillments.
6.   National and cosmic implications are more frequent than individual ones.
7.   Not every detail of extraordinary descriptions has interpretive significance.
